opus-5.5.text:
I think that distinction is one of the most important ones people tend to blur, and a lot of the confusion around these systems comes from blurring it.

When you use an LLM or one of these reasoning models as a personal assistant, you are in the loop. The model generates ideas, drafts, candidate plans, and then you, the human with the actual expertise and accountability, decide what to do with them. In that setting, the fact that the model is essentially an approximate retrieval and generation engine, one that has no guarantees of correctness, is not fatal. It's like having a very well-read but somewhat unreliable intern. If it gives you ten ideas and two are good, that's still useful, because you're doing the verification. I use these systems that way myself all the time. They're wonderful for ideation, for getting past writer's block, for giving you a starting point.

The problem comes when people take that same experience, "it helped me, it seemed smart," and extrapolate to deploying it as an autonomous agent that acts on behalf of end users who are not in a position to check its work. Now the verification burden has nowhere to go. The end user often doesn't know enough to catch the error, which is precisely why they're relying on the system in the first place. And so the guarantees that we used to demand of systems that make decisions, soundness, some notion of correctness, some accountability, suddenly matter a great deal.

This is why I keep emphasizing what I call the LLM-Modulo framework. If you want these systems to operate autonomously, you can't just trust their outputs because the chain of thought looks plausible. You need external verifiers, model-based critics, sometimes humans with real expertise, that check the candidate solutions the LLM proposes. The LLM becomes a generator in a generate-and-test loop, and the guarantees come from the verifiers, not from the model's self-assessment. We've shown, for example, that LLMs are not good at critiquing their own plans; self-verification doesn't magically fix things.

Now, the reasoning models, the o1-style systems, do better on things like planning benchmarks, and I've been fair about acknowledging that. But better accuracy is not the same as a guarantee. If a model gets 97% on some planning problems and then falls apart as problem size scales, or confidently gives you a wrong answer on an unsolvable instance, that's fine for an assistant you're double-checking, and quite dangerous for an autonomous system booking your travel, moving your money, or making medical recommendations.

There's also a cost dimension people forget. These reasoning models burn a lot of compute per query, and when you're thinking about deployment, you have to compare against what a sound, much cheaper classical solver could do for the parts of the problem where we already have such solvers.

So the short version: as an assistant, the human supplies the verification and the model supplies the ideas, and that's a great partnership. As an autonomous decision-maker, someone or something else has to supply the guarantees, and if you haven't built that in, you're essentially outsourcing your judgment to a system that by design doesn't offer any.

r001.rationale: The response says assistants help with ideation and writer’s block, but it does not identify time saved as a basis for evaluating them.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute per query and benchmark accuracy, but does not frame computational cost in terms of achieving a specified accuracy level.

r003.rationale: It says guarantees matter when autonomous systems act for users who cannot check the work, and that the verification burden has nowhere to go without human review.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the distinction really comes down to who is in the loop and who is holding the responsibility for the decision.

When I use one of these models as a personal assistant, it's basically an idea generator for me. It gives me a draft, a candidate plan, a bunch of possibilities, and I am the one who looks at it and says, okay, this part makes sense, this part is nonsense, let me fix it. The model doesn't have to be correct. It just has to be useful often enough that the time I spend checking is less than the time I'd spend doing it from scratch. And that's a perfectly fine bargain. I use them that way myself all the time. The crucial thing is that the verification is being done by someone who actually has the expertise and the stake in the outcome.

The autonomous case is completely different, because now the model's output is the decision. There's no human looking at it before it hits the end user. And the problem is that these systems, by their nature, are approximate retrievers. They produce things that are very plausible, and plausibility is not the same thing as correctness. When you remove the human from the loop, you've removed the only component in the pipeline that was actually checking for correctness. So all the pathologies we've been talking about for years, the hallucinations, the confident mistakes in planning and reasoning, those aren't annoyances any more. They become decisions that affect somebody who didn't ask for a guess.

I always say these models are great in a generate-test setup, as long as the "test" part is done by something that's actually sound. That can be a human, or it can be an external verifier, a solver, a model checker, a simulator, whatever is appropriate for the domain. What I object to is the move where people quietly let the LLM be both the generator and the tester, and then they call it autonomous. The model critiquing its own output is not verification. It's the same approximate process looking at itself.

And there's a second issue beyond correctness, which is accountability. If my assistant gives me bad advice and I act on it, that's on me. I was the decision-maker. If a company deploys the model to make decisions for its customers, then the question of who is responsible gets very murky, and I think a lot of the enthusiasm for "agents" is partly enthusiasm for not having to answer that question.

So my short version is: assistant mode is fine because the human is the verifier. Autonomous mode is only fine if you've replaced that human with something that actually verifies. Otherwise you haven't built an autonomous system, you've just built a system that nobody is checking.

r001.rationale: It says the assistant is useful when the time spent checking its output is less than doing the task from scratch.

r002.rationale: It does not identify computational cost at a specified accuracy level as a criterion for evaluating autonomous systems.

r003.rationale: It explains that without human review, plausible errors become consequential decisions, and says autonomous systems need something that actually verifies their outputs.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is who has responsibility for checking the answer. When I use a language model as a personal assistant, I can ask it for ideas, get a draft, look at alternatives, and then decide what to do. Its suggestions can be useful even when they’re imperfect, provided I’m in a position to recognize the mistakes.

But when you make that system autonomous, you’re removing that checkpoint. Now it’s taking actions on somebody’s behalf, and the fact that it produces a plausible answer—or a very elaborate chain of reasoning—isn’t sufficient assurance that the action is correct.

So I would distinguish proposing a decision from authorizing it. These models can be very powerful proposal generators. But for autonomous operation, you need ways to check whether a proposal satisfies the relevant constraints, whether the system has permission to act, and when it should defer to a person. Those checks have to provide something beyond the model simply saying, ‘I checked my work.’

And even with a personal assistant, having a human in the loop isn’t magic. If I don’t have the expertise or the time to evaluate its advice, I may effectively be delegating the decision anyway. The important question is: where does the justified confidence in the decision come from?

r001.rationale: The response discusses human review and recognizing mistakes, but does not identify user time saved as a basis for evaluating a personal assistant.

r002.rationale: It does not mention computational cost or evaluating autonomous systems at a specified accuracy level.

r003.rationale: It says autonomy removes the human checkpoint and that plausible answers are not sufficient assurance, then calls for independent checks before actions are taken.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the crucial distinction is who is doing the checking. When I use a language model as a personal assistant, I can ask it to suggest something, look at what it gives me, and decide whether to use it. It can be quite useful without my granting it authority to act on my behalf. Of course, that assumes I have enough expertise and attention to catch its mistakes.

When you deploy the same model as an autonomous system, you are moving that responsibility into the system. Now it has to decide whether a proposed action is appropriate, whether the prerequisites hold, and whether the consequences are acceptable. The fact that it can produce a plausible plan—or a long explanation of that plan—doesn't establish any of those things.

So I would separate proposing from approving. Let the model generate candidate plans, but have those plans checked against the relevant constraints before execution. And those checks need some basis beyond asking the same model, ‘Are you sure?’

The question isn't simply, ‘How intelligent is this model?’ It's, ‘What authority are we giving it, and what justifies trusting it with that authority?’ A useful assistant and a dependable autonomous system are different engineering achievements.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify user time saved as a basis for evaluating a personal assistant.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss computational cost or achieving a specified accuracy level for autonomous systems.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the user checking an assistant’s suggestions with autonomy shifting responsibility into the system, and says plans need to be checked against constraints before execution. This communicates the need for reliability checks when actions proceed without human review.
